claim: C13 extension removes all parameter calibration for the common-ell staircase family, while allowing arbitrary independent phases on the two rays. A balanced pair of exact flow clocks has crossing cost delta with tau+delta< s_r; summing the actual recursive word yields a uniform normalized gap <=(c^3/a)c^(-m). This covers every ell>=1, every initial point, all knot visits and crossing patterns, and horizon-dependent finite trajectory-preserving realizations; it still does not cover arbitrary scalar profiles.
evidence:
# A full log-periodic staircase class is controlled by scalar flow time

Status: complete scoped candidate proof, not verifier-accepted. No new verifier
call. Unlike the earlier geometric-grid relay bound, this result puts no
restriction on the crossing pattern, knot visits, or gradients within ordinary
blocks. It covers the entire explicitly specified function class below, with
parameters and finite realizations allowed to depend on the horizon. It does
not cover every scalar convex smooth function or the unrestricted W_n.

## 1. The recursive schedules and a legal multiscale derivative

Set c=13/5, a=c^(-17), b_u=a c^u, H_0=(), and

    H_(m+1)=(H_m,b_m,H_m),
    s_u=sum H_u=a(c^u-2^u)/(c-2).

Fix integers m>=r>=17, and write b=b_r, S=s_r, and J=m-r. Put eta=13/8.
Since (10/13)^3<1/2 and (10/13)^2<4/5,
(10/13)^17<1/40. Therefore S>=eta b.

Choose, independently for each ray sigma in {+,-}, a positive phase theta_sigma
and a parameter ell_sigma satisfying

    b <= ell_sigma <= 1+(S-log c)/(c-1).                     (1)

This interval is nonempty: at ell=b its associated expression
(c-1)(b-1)+log c is smaller than S, since
eta-(c-1)=1/40 and log c<1<c-1. Define

    u_sigma=c ell_sigma-(c-1),
    M_(sigma,z)=theta_sigma c^z,          z any integer.

On ray sigma, prescribe gradient magnitude G_sigma as follows. For each z,
let M=M_(sigma,z) and put

    G_sigma(R)=M,
       ell_sigma M <= R <= u_sigma M;

    G_sigma(R)=R-(u_sigma-1)M,
       u_sigma M <= R <= c ell_sigma M.                     (2)

The second interval is the ramp from gradient M to cM. Its outer endpoint is
the next plateau's inner endpoint. These intervals cover every positive R;
their endpoints agree. Set G_sigma(0)=0.

The profile is continuous, nondecreasing, and 1-Lipschitz, with slopes zero
or one. It satisfies

    G_sigma(cR)=c G_sigma(R),
    0<=G_sigma(R)<=R/ell_sigma<=R/b.                        (3)

For the secant inequality on a ramp, write G=R-(u_sigma-1)M. The ratio G/R
increases to 1/ell_sigma at the ramp's outer endpoint; on a plateau the ratio
is at most its inner-endpoint value 1/ell_sigma. Thus (3) holds everywhere.
Continuity at zero follows from (3).

Define g(x)=G_+(x) for x>=0 and g(x)=-G_-(-x) for x<=0, and define

    f(x)=integral_0^x g(t) dt.

This is one globally fixed convex differentiable 1-smooth function, with
f(0)=0=min f. Across opposite rays, the Lipschitz inequality follows from
G_+(R)+G_-(T)<=R+T. The phases and parameters of the two rays need not agree.
There is no fixed quadratic neighborhood of zero; the knots accumulate there.

## 2. Exact areas and finite versions of the same trajectory

Write ell=ell_sigma and

    K_sigma=1/2+(ell-1)/(c+1).

At the inner endpoint ell M of any plateau,

    f(sigma ell M)=K_sigma M^2.                            (4)

All ramps below that endpoint together traverse gradient magnitudes from
zero to M and contribute M^2/2. The lower plateaus contribute

    (c-1)(ell-1)M^2 sum_(j>=1)c^(-2j)
       =[(ell-1)/(c+1)]M^2,

which proves (4). On the plateau itself,

    f(sigma R)=K_sigma M^2+M(R-ell M).                       (5)

On the following ramp, start with (5) at R=u_sigma M and add
[G_sigma(R)^2-M^2]/2. These are complete areas, including every inner level.
In particular f(sigma cR)=c^2 f(sigma R).

For any one finite nonzero trajectory, a finite-knot function can realize
exactly the same gradients and values. On each ray choose an inner plateau
endpoint ell M below every nonzero sampled radius. Replace the profile below
it by a zero segment up to

    delta=[c/(c+1)](ell-1)M,

then a slope-one ramp of length M, then a plateau at M up to ell M. The
endpoint gradient remains M, and the enclosed area is

    ell M^2-delta M-M^2/2=K_sigma M^2.

Thus all larger-radius gradients and values remain unchanged. Extend the
outermost needed plateau to a cap beyond all sampled radii. This produces
a globally legal finite-knot function and the identical full GD trajectory,
with the same fixed minimizer zero and the same initial-distance normalization.
The number of retained levels may grow with the horizon. This is a trajectory
preserving truncation; arbitrary unrelated core replacements are not claimed
to preserve the bound proved below.

## 3. Every ordinary block contracts by one complete radial period

For either ray, the exact flow time across one multiplicative period is

    integral_(R/c)^R dt/G_sigma(t)
        = tau_sigma :=(c-1)(ell_sigma-1)+log c.              (6)

It is independent of R. Indeed G_sigma(ct)=cG_sigma(t) makes this integral
periodic in log R with a full-period integration window. Evaluating from
ell_sigma M to c ell_sigma M gives plateau time u_sigma-ell_sigma and ramp
time log c, which proves (6). Condition (1) says tau_sigma<=S.

Every step of H_r is at most b/c. By (3), such a step h takes a nonzero
radius R to a strictly positive smaller radius R'=R-hG_sigma(R), with
R'>=(1-1/c)R. Therefore there are no sign crossings within any H_r block,
regardless of its starting radius or how many knots it traverses.

For each of its steps, monotonicity gives

    integral_(R')^R dt/G_sigma(t)
        >= (R-R')/G_sigma(R)=h.                             (7)

Add (7) across the full block. If its input and output radii are A and B,
the flow time integral from B to A is at least S>=tau_sigma. By (6) and
positivity of the integrand, B<=A/c. Hence every H_r, from every point on
either ray, satisfies

    |x_after H_r| <= |x_before H_r|/c.                      (8)

No endpoint is selected separately at successive steps. This is a bound
on every actual trajectory of the fixed function (2), and consequently on
its complete interval image as well.

## 4. Exact coarse-word bookkeeping and the objective bound

The exact decomposition of H_m has 2^J copies of H_r and 2^J-1 checkpoint
steps. A level k checkpoint has h=b c^k and occurs 2^(J-k-1) times,
for 0<=k<=J-1. At such a step, (3) gives

    |x-hg(x)| <= max(1,h/b-1)|x| <= c^k |x|.                (9)

This allows a crossing, a same-sign step, or a zero landing. No prescribed
crossing pattern is used. The total checkpoint exponent is

    sum_(k=0)^(J-1) k 2^(J-k-1)=2^J-J-1.

Combining every copy of (8) with every copy of (9) yields

    |x_(2^m-1)| <= c^(-J-1)|x_0|.                         (10)

When J=0 the formula is just (8); the empty sum convention is consistent.
Finally (3) implies f(x)<=x^2/(2b) by integration from the fixed minimizer.
Therefore every initial point and every function specified by (1)-(2) obey

    2f(x_(2^m-1))/|x_0|^2
        <= b^(-1)c^(-2J-2)
        = a^(-1)c^(-m-J-2)
        <= [1/(a c^2)]c^(-m).                             (11)

The bound is uniform in r, both phases, both admissible ell parameters and
the initial point. These choices can all depend on m. The finite trajectory
preserving versions of Section 2 have the identical objective ratio.

## 5. Comparison with the exact profile and the remaining gap

A self-contained rough exact-DP estimate suffices. For C_n=S_circle(n)+1
and D_n=2S_bullet(n)+1, the shifted joins are

    Omega(A,B)=(A+B+sqrt((A+B)^2+4AB))/2,
    G(A,D)=2A+D/2+sqrt(D^2+8AD)/2.

The inequality Omega(A,B)<=(A^(3/4)+B^(3/4))^(4/3) is equivalent to
t^(4/3)+(1-t)^(4/3)+[t(1-t)]^(4/3)<=1. To prove it put
x=t^(1/3), y=(1-t)^(1/3). The difference from 1 is
x^3y^3[1/(1+x+x^2)+1/(1+y+y^2)-xy]>=0, since each reciprocal is at least
1/3 and xy<=2^(-2/3)<2/3. Induction gives C_n<=(n+1)^(4/3). The estimate
G(A,D)<=D+4A and u^(4/3)+v^(4/3)<=(u+v)^(4/3) give D_n<=1+4n^(4/3).
Since c^3>16, multiplying (11) by D_(2^m-1) proves that the supremum
objective ratio in this class, divided by U_(2^m-1)^ZJ, tends to zero.

The profile class has arbitrary numbers of knots, asymmetric ray phases,
multiple visits, and ordinary blocks that can traverse many knots. Its
limitation is instead its precise discrete homogeneity and the calibrated
flow-time/secant range (1). Functions outside that range, nonperiodic radial
geometry, and the complete scalar class remain open. A scalar class bound
does not upper-bound the unrestricted multidimensional W; the already shared
coupled-coordinate divergent example remains compatible with this result.

## 6. The calibration restriction can be removed for a common staircase parameter

The following extension covers EVERY ell>=1 in the profile (2), with
ell_+=ell_-=ell, while keeping theta_+ and theta_- completely independent.
There is no condition (1), no prescribed crossing pattern, and no restriction
on the initial point. The number of knots, phases, ell, and the finite
trajectory-preserving truncations can all depend on m.

For every m>=17 this larger class satisfies the uniform bound

    2f(x_(2^m-1))/|x_0|^2 <= (c^3/a)c^(-m).                (12)

It consequently also has vanishing ratio to the exact U_(2^m-1)^ZJ, by
the elementary benchmark estimate already proved in Section 5.

### 6.1 Choose the coarse scale and define the two flow clocks

Choose the smallest r>=17 for which b=b_r>=ell. Then b/c<ell<=b; the strict
left inequality also holds when ell=1 and r=17. Set S=s_r. Every step in H_r
is at most b/c, and hence preserves sign by the bound |g(x)|<=|x|/ell.

If m<r, the entire H_m preserves sign. Put w=|g(x_n)| and R=|x_n|. Then
R+s_m w<=|x_0|, while f(x_n)<=Rw-w^2/2. Completing the square gives

    2f(x_n)/|x_0|^2 <=1/(1+2s_m)
       <=[1/(2eta a)]c^(-m),

which is smaller than (12). Hence assume m>=r and put J=m-r.

Reflect the function if needed so that x_0>0. Multiplying a phase theta_sigma
by c does not change its derivative profile. We can therefore choose phase
representatives theta_+=theta and theta_-=q theta with 1<=q<c.

Let G be the template (2) with plateau heights c^z and common parameter ell,
and define its signed flow coordinate on R>0 by

    F(R)=integral_ell^R dt/G(t).

The integral is negative when R<ell. Put

    tau=(c-1)(ell-1)+log c,
    E=(c-1)-log c>0,
    F_+(R)=F(R/theta),       F_-(R)=F(R/(q theta)).

Then F_sigma(cR)=F_sigma(R)+tau. Each positive or negative H_r block reduces
its own flow clock by at least S, by the stepwise integral inequality (7).

### 6.2 Exact worst crossing-clock costs

Define

    D_+=F(b/q),       D_-=F(bq),
    delta=(D_++D_-)/2,
    v=(D_--D_+)/2,
    P_+(R)=F_+(R),    P_-(R)=F_-(R)+v.                    (13)

For a step h=b c^k that crosses from ray sigma to the other ray, its landing
radius is h G_sigma(R)-R<=h G_sigma(R). Its change in the unadjusted clock
is therefore at most

    k tau + F_other(b G_sigma(R))-F_sigma(R).              (14)

The final difference in (14) is maximized at an inner plateau endpoint.
On a plateau its first term is constant and its second increases with R,
so the difference decreases. On a unit-slope ramp, use the current gradient
u as coordinate; then dR/du=1 and its derivative is

    b/G_other(bu)-1/u >=(ell-1)/u>=0,

by the secant bound G_other(y)<=y/ell. Thus it increases on a ramp. At all
inner plateau endpoints on one ray the difference has the same value, by
the common radial period and common tau. That value is exactly D_+ or D_-
from (13). The additive constant v therefore makes BOTH crossing directions
have adjusted-clock change at most k tau+delta.

This same bound also holds for a checkpoint that does not cross. Its clock
decreases by at least h>=b, by (7). Since b/q>=ell/c and bq>=ell,

    delta>=-tau/2>-b,

where tau<(c-1)ell<2b. Consequently -b<=k tau+delta for every k>=0.
A zero landing has zero terminal objective and needs no logarithmic clock.
We have proved, for every nonzero trajectory and every checkpoint,

    change of P <= k tau+delta.                            (15)

### 6.3 Uniform bound on the phase-dependent cost

We now prove

    tau+delta <=(c-1)b<S.                                 (16)

This quantitative inequality is essential; it is not an assumed profile
closure. Put p=b/ell, so 1<=p<c. For 1<=z<=c, the template gradient is at
least 1 on [ell,ell z], whence

    F(ell z)<=ell(z-1),       tau=(c-1)ell-E.               (17)

Reduce p q and p/q by powers of c into z_1,z_2 in [1,c]. Let K be the sum
of those two powers. Then

    z_1 z_2=p^2/c^K,
    2delta<=K tau+ell(z_1+z_2-2).                          (18)

For z_1,z_2 in [1,c], their sum is at most 1+z_1z_2 when the product is
at most c, and at most c+(z_1z_2)/c when the product is at least c.
These follow respectively from (z_1-1)(z_2-1)>=0 and
(c-z_1)(c-z_2)>=0.

If 1<=p<=sqrt(c), the possible K are -1 and 0. Applying these two sum bounds
in (18) gives

    delta <=[ell(p^2-1)+E]/2.

Therefore

    tau+delta <=ell[p^2/2+c-3/2]-E/2 <=(c-1)b.

The last inequality is equivalent, after dropping the favorable E/2, to
(p-1)(p-(2c-3))<=0. It holds because sqrt(c)<2c-3 for c=13/5.

If sqrt(c)<=p<c, the possible K are 0 and 1. The same calculation gives

    delta <=ell[c-2+p^2/c]/2,
    tau+delta <=ell[3c/2-2+p^2/(2c)]-E <=(c-1)b.

For the last inequality, the difference divided by ell, before the favorable
-E term, is the convex quadratic
p^2/(2c)-(c-1)p+3c/2-2. At p=sqrt(c) it equals
(c-1)(3/2-sqrt(c))<0; at p=c it equals -(c-1)(c-2)<0.
Convexity therefore makes it nonpositive on the full interval. This proves
the first inequality in (16). The second follows from S>=eta b and
eta=13/8>c-1=8/5.

### 6.4 Complete clock recurrence and normalization

There are 2^J ordinary H_r blocks, the checkpoint level sum is
2^J-J-1, and the number of checkpoints is 2^J-1. Adding all actual clock
changes using (15) gives

    P_final-P_initial
       <=-2^J[S-tau-delta]-(J+1)tau-delta
       <=-(J+1)tau-delta.                                 (19)

All crossing histories and all ray changes are included. The two clocks
differ from a common reference by a controlled phase amount: since
q in [1,c), one has F_+(R)-tau<=F_-(R)<=F_+(R), and 0<=v<=tau.
The latter follows because D_--D_+=F(bq)-F(b/q)<=2tau.
Thus, for either final ray, P_final>=F_+(|x_n|)-tau, whereas
P_initial=F_+(|x_0|). Together with delta>=-tau/2, (19) yields

    F_+(|x_n|)-F_+(|x_0|) <=-(J-1/2)tau
                                  <=-(J-1)tau.

The clock is increasing and has period increment tau, so

    |x_n|<=c^(1-J)|x_0|.

This bound is deliberately loose when J=0, but remains valid. The global
secant bound gives f(x)<=x^2/(2ell), and b/c<ell implies

    2f(x_n)/|x_0|^2
        <=ell^(-1)c^(2-2J)
        <=b^(-1)c^(3-2J)
        =a^(-1)c^(-m)c^(3-J)
        <=(c^3/a)c^(-m),

which proves (12).

The remaining restriction is genuine discrete radial homogeneity with factor
c and a COMMON ell on both rays. Their phases are arbitrary. Section 1 also
allows different ell values in its stated calibrated range. These results
do not cover arbitrary independently scaled rays outside that range,
different radial periods, nonperiodic knot geometry, or the entire scalar
class. The full multidimensional exact-profile target remains unresolved.

claim: C14 full-class extension: EVERY even scalar convex 1-smooth profile with g((13/5)R)=(13/5)g(R), allowing arbitrary within-period shape and horizon-dependent complexity, obeys normalized GD gap <=(1/(a c))c^(-m) on H_m. evidence:
# Arbitrary even profiles with discrete radial homogeneity are too weak on H_m

Status: complete scoped candidate proof, not verifier-accepted. No verifier
call. This extends the fixed-staircase analysis to every shape within a radial
period. Evenness and the stated exact discrete homogeneity are essential
hypotheses; the full scalar and multidimensional classes remain unresolved.

## 1. Statement

Let c=13/5, a=c^(-17), b_u=a c^u, and

    H_0=(),  H_(m+1)=(H_m,b_m,H_m),
    N_m=2^m-1,
    s_m=sum H_m=a(c^m-2^m)/(c-2).

Consider ANY nondecreasing 1-Lipschitz function g:[0,infinity)->[0,infinity)
with g(0)=0 and

    g(cR)=c g(R),                         R>=0.              (1)

Extend it oddly to the real line and set
f(x)=integral_0^|x| g(R)dR. This gives an even convex differentiable
1-smooth function with fixed minimum f(0)=0. No prescribed plateau, ramp,
curvature pattern, knot count, or sign-crossing history is assumed.

For every m>=17, every x_0!=0, and the complete GD schedule H_m,

    2f(x_(N_m))/|x_0|^2 <= [1/(a c)]c^(-m).                (2)

The function g itself may depend on the entire horizon m. Consequently the
supremum of these objective ratios over the full class (1), divided by the
exact U_(N_m)^ZJ, tends to zero. This is a class obstruction, not a bound
on the unrestricted W_(N_m)(H_m).

## 2. A scalar clock and the quantitative closure inequality

The identically zero g has zero objective. Otherwise g(R)>0 for every R>0:
if it vanished at one positive radius, (1) and monotonicity would make it
vanish on arbitrarily large intervals. The continuous ratio g(R)/R is
periodic in log R. Thus its maximum M>0 is attained on any multiplicative
period, and M<=1 by smoothness. Put ell=1/M>=1.

Define a flow clock

    F(R)=integral_1^R dt/g(t),        R>0.

The arbitrary reference 1 affects only an additive constant. Equation (1)
implies that

    F(cR)-F(R)=tau>0                                        (3)

is independent of R: differentiate in R, or substitute t=cu. Choose r>=17
minimal with b=b_r>=ell. Then b/c<ell<=b. Define

    D=max_(R>0) [F(b g(R))-F(R)].                           (4)

The expression in brackets is periodic under R->cR, so the maximum exists
on a compact radial period. At a maximizer of g(R)/R=1/ell, one has
b g(R)>=R. Therefore D>=0.

The key proved inequality is

    tau+D <=(c-1)b.                                        (5)

Here is a direct proof for every possible input radius; no functional
inequality is left as an assumption. Fix R>0, put u=g(R)>0 and q=R/u>=1.

If q<=b, monotonicity gives

    F(bu)-F(R)<=b-q.                                       (6)

On the period [R,cR], the endpoint gradients are u and cu. Monotonicity and
the 1-Lipschitz condition give the pointwise lower bound

    g(t)>=max(u, cu-(cR-t)).

The switch occurs at t=cR-(c-1)u>=R. Integrating the reciprocal of this
lower bound yields

    tau<= (c-1)(q-1)+log c.                                (7)

Adding (6)-(7) gives

    tau+F(bu)-F(R)
       <=b+(c-2)q-(c-1)+log c
       <=(c-1)b-(c-1)+log c <(c-1)b,

because q<=b, c>2 and log c<c-1.

If q>=b, use (3) to write the same quantity as

    tau+F(bu)-F(R)=F(cbu)-F(R).

When cbu<R this quantity is negative. Otherwise every point of integration
has gradient at least u, so it is at most cb-q<=(c-1)b. This proves (5)
uniformly in R, and hence for the actual maximum D in (4).

## 3. Actual block and checkpoint updates of the same clock

Every step of H_r is at most b/c<ell. Since g(R)<=R/ell, these steps cannot
cross zero from a nonzero point. For a positive-radius step
R'=R-hg(R)>0, monotonicity gives

    F(R)-F(R')=integral_(R')^R dt/g(t)
        >=(R-R')/g(R)=h.                                  (8)

The same calculation applies after reflecting a negative point, because f
is even. Therefore each actual H_r block decreases the clock of the absolute
radius by at least S=s_r.

For a checkpoint of level k, h=b c^k, consider the actual next radius.
If it does not cross zero, its clock decreases. If it crosses, then

    R'=h g(R)-R <= c^k b g(R).

By (3)-(4), this gives

    F(R')-F(R)<=k tau+D.                                   (9)

Since D>=0, (9) also bounds a same-sign checkpoint. A zero landing has zero
terminal objective and can be excluded from the clock calculation.

For r>=17, one has S>=eta b with eta=13/8. To check this directly, note
(10/13)^3<1/2 and (10/13)^2<4/5, hence (10/13)^17<1/40; substitute in
s_r/b_r=[1-(2/c)^r]/(c-2). Since eta>c-1=8/5, (5) gives

    S-tau-D>0.                                            (10)

Thus the growing-state flow description has a genuine, uniformly profitable
update. It is not just a restatement of the unknown scalar optimization.

## 4. Sum the exact recursive word and retain the original normalization

First suppose m>=r and put J=m-r. The word H_m contains 2^J copies of H_r.
Its checkpoint levels k=0,...,J-1 occur 2^(J-k-1) times. Their total level
sum is 2^J-J-1, and their number is 2^J-1. Adding (8)-(9) along the full
actual trajectory gives

    F(|x_(N_m)|)-F(|x_0|)
       <=-2^J S+(2^J-J-1)tau+(2^J-1)D
       =-2^J(S-tau-D)-(J+1)tau-D
       <=-(J+1)tau.                                      (11)

Equation (3) and monotonicity of F imply

    |x_(N_m)|<=c^(-J-1)|x_0|.                             (12)

The global secant bound g(R)<=R/ell supplies the complete area bound
f(x)<=x^2/(2ell). Since ell>b/c,

    2f(x_(N_m))/|x_0|^2
       <=ell^(-1)c^(-2J-2)
       <=b^(-1)c^(-2J-1)
       =a^(-1)c^(-m-J-1)
       <=[1/(a c)]c^(-m).                                (13)

If m<r, every step in H_m is smaller than ell and the entire trajectory
stays on its initial ray. Let w=g(|x_(N_m)|) and R=|x_(N_m)|. Monotonicity
and smoothness give R+s_m w<=|x_0| and f(x_(N_m))<=Rw-w^2/2. Thus

    2f(x_(N_m))/|x_0|^2<=1/(1+2s_m)
       <=[1/(2eta a)]c^(-m)
       <=[1/(a c)]c^(-m),

using m>=17 and 2eta>c. This proves (2) in every case. All distances refer
to the same fixed minimizer zero. Scaling f by L gives exactly the project's
normalization and GD steps h_t/L.

## 5. Explicit exact-profile comparison and finite-knot realizations

For completeness set C_n=S_circle(n)+1 and D_n=2S_bullet(n)+1. Their shifted
joins are Omega(A,B)=(A+B+sqrt((A+B)^2+4AB))/2 and
G(A,D)=2A+D/2+sqrt(D^2+8AD)/2. The bound
Omega(A,B)<=(A^(3/4)+B^(3/4))^(4/3) reduces to
t^(4/3)+(1-t)^(4/3)+[t(1-t)]^(4/3)<=1. With x=t^(1/3),y=(1-t)^(1/3),
the difference from 1 is x^3 y^3[1/(1+x+x^2)+1/(1+y+y^2)-xy]>=0:
both reciprocal terms are at least 1/3 and xy<=2^(-2/3)<2/3. Induction gives
C_n<=(n+1)^(4/3). Since G(A,D)<=D+4A and the power 4/3 is superadditive on
nonnegative inputs, the dominant DP gives D_n<=1+4n^(4/3). Multiplying (2)
by D_(N_m) proves the claimed vanishing ratio, because c^3>16.

If the profile has finitely many affine pieces within one radial period,
any one finite nonzero trajectory has a finite-knot realization preserving
all its values and gradients. Choose a radius R below every nonzero query
and terminal radius, and put u=g(R)>0 and A=f(R). Smoothness and monotonicity
give

    u^2/2<=A<=Ru-u^2/2.

Replace the inner profile by zero up to
delta=R-u/2-A/u, then a unit-slope ramp of length u, then a plateau at u up
to R. The displayed bounds imply 0<=delta<=R-u. Its terminal gradient is u
and its area is Ru-delta u-u^2/2=A. All larger-radius gradients and values
are therefore unchanged. Apply the same replacement on both rays and cap
outside the largest sampled radius. The original finite GD trajectory and
its exact objective normalization are preserved. This does not claim that
an arbitrary nonhomogeneous core replacement obeys the same global theorem.

The new obstruction includes arbitrary legal within-period geometry,
horizon-dependent shape and scale, dense gradient values, arbitrarily many
knots, and every crossing pattern. It is still restricted to even functions
with the exact radial period c=13/5. The independently phased staircase
result in research/max3_multiscale_flow_obstruction.md remains a separate
asymmetric extension. Neither result decides the full scalar class or the
project's unrestricted all-schedule minimax problem.

claim: Exact enlargement of the geometric state to legal minimum-raising joins: retain the two-parameter sublevel distance Xi(t,r), update it by a one-variable quadratic infimum, and recenter ALL past values by the actual common minimum. evidence:
# Exact sublevel state for joins that raise the minimum

Status: UNVERIFIED joint proof and counterexample, worker max, 2026-09-26.
No verification call is allocated. This does not assert the unrestricted
Zhang--Jiang comparison. It extends the zero-preserving state test rather
than contradicting its explicitly restricted sufficiency statement.

## 1. What the zero-level profile loses

For a finite convex polyhedral function J on a Euclidean space, write
env J(x)=min_z[J(z)+||x-z||^2/2]. All functions below have an attained
minimum. The unique minimizing z is the proximal point. If x-z is the
gradient of an affine plane active in J at z, the subgradient inequality
and the strict quadratic term show that z is the unique proximal point.
Moreover env J is convex, differentiable, and has 1-Lipschitz gradient
x-z. One direct proof of the Lipschitz assertion adds the two proximal
subgradient inequalities, obtaining
||g(x)-g(x')||^2 <= <g(x)-g(x'),x-x'>.
The minimizing inequalities give differentiability with this gradient.
Finally min env J=min J and their minimizer sets coincide: equality in
J(z)+||x-z||^2/2 >= min J requires x=z and J(z)=min J.

Consider the two functions on coordinates (t,y)

    J_A(t,y)=max(0,1-t,-y),
    J_B(t,y)=max(0,1-t,-y,3(1-t-y)/4).

Both have precisely the zero set {t>=1,y>=0}. Start at x_init=(-1,-7)
and take the one-step prefix h=(7). Both functions have the same legal
proximal samples:

    query x_0=(-1,-7), proximal z_0=(-1,-6), height V_0=6,
    gradient g_0=(0,-1);
    query x_1=(-1,0), proximal p=(0,0), height V_1=1,
    gradient g_1=(-1,0).

At z_0 the values of (0,1-t,-y,3(1-t-y)/4) are (0,2,6,6).
At p they are (0,1,0,3/4). Thus the selected gradients really are
active-plane subgradients for both functions. The GD equality
x_0-7g_0=x_1 holds. Set u=(1,0), so the same boundary gradient is
-m_boundary u with m_boundary=1.

The entire proposed state, including the added gradient magnitude, agrees:

    Phi(t)=max(0,1-t),
    Psi(s)=min(1,6+s),
    Dist(t)=(t+1)^2+49 for t>=1, and +infinity otherwise.       (1)

Here Phi(t)=J(p+tu), Psi(s)=min_i[V_i-s<u,z_i-p>], and Dist is
the squared distance from the same x_init to the zero slice at t.
In fact all prefix queries, gradients, heights, initial points, boundary
points, and zero sets agree, a stronger equality than the state requires.

Append the identical fresh-coordinate cell in a new coordinate w. Choose
bridge b=3/2, scale d=1/2, cap c=1, endpoint epsilon=1/2, local initial
query (epsilon,-1), and no ordinary steps. Its center, common plane
height, and two planes are

    p_new=(1/4,0,1/2),   F_cell=13/16,
    C(t,y,w)=11/16+t/2,
    E(t,y,w)=1+t/4-w/2.

These are exactly F_cell+d<t-axis,z-p_new> and
F_cell+d<(epsilon,0,-1),z-p_new>. For T=A,B define

    Jbar_T=max(J_T,C,E).

The old query x_1 is sent by the prescribed bridge to x_2=(1/2,0,0).
At p_new the two new planes both equal 13/16, while both old functions
equal 3/4. Therefore g_2=(1/4,0,-1/2) is an active normal and
x_2=p_new+g_2. The new planes at the two old proximal points have values

    at z_0=(-1,-6,0): C=3/16, E=3/4, both <=6;
    at p=(0,0,0):     C=11/16, E=1, both <=1.

This checks both directions of every cross-block comparison. All gradients
and all GD iterates are actual gradients and iterates of env Jbar_T.

Nevertheless neither Jbar_T has a zero. Indeed its minimum is

    mu=19/24,

because its planes 1-t and 11/16+t/2 have minimum possible maximum
19/24, attained only when t=5/24. At that t the endpoint constraint is
w>=25/48. The remaining minimum-set constraints are exactly

    argmin Jbar_A={t=5/24, y>=-19/24, w>=25/48},
    argmin Jbar_B={t=5/24, y>=-19/72, w>=25/48}.              (2)

For B, the extra inequality is
(3/4)(19/24-y)<=19/24, equivalent to y>=-19/72; it dominates
y>=-19/24. Every displayed point satisfies all the other planes, proving
both attainment and the complete descriptions in (2).

The actual closest minimizers to (-1,-7,0) are thus the respective corners,
and their squared distances are

    R_A^2=(29/24)^2+(149/24)^2+(25/48)^2=30931/768,
    R_B^2=(29/24)^2+(485/72)^2+(25/48)^2=976801/20736.       (3)

Both have F_cell-mu=1/48>0 and ||g_2||^2=5/16. Their normalized last
errors for the identical schedule (7,3/2) are therefore different:

    2(env Jbar_A(x_2)-mu)/R_A^2 =272/30931,
    2(env Jbar_B(x_2)-mu)/R_B^2 =7344/976801.                (4)

Subtracting the same mu from the WHOLE respective functions normalizes
their minima to zero and changes none of their GD iterates. Every retained
past function value is reduced by that same constant. This is not an
independent reset of a checkpoint value.

Conclusion: Phi,Psi,Dist and m_boundary cannot determine the true distance
normalization of a minimum-raising join for general allowed polyhedral
histories. The previous zero-preserving rule correctly rejects this join;
its restricted sufficiency is unaffected. The stronger rule that accepts
all legal joins needs more information than the zero slice.

## 2. The missing information can be written explicitly

Define the two-parameter sublevel distance profile

    Xi(t,r)=min{||x_init-z||^2:J(z)<=r, <u,z-p>=t},          (5)

with value +infinity when the set is empty. Extend it by +infinity for
r<0 when min J=0. The minimum exists whenever feasible: the feasible
set is closed and the squared norm is coercive.

For the preceding two histories, for r>=0 and t>=1-r the exact profiles
are

    Xi_A(t,r)=(t+1)^2+max(0,7-r)^2,
    Xi_B(t,r)=(t+1)^2+max(0,7-r,8-t-4r/3)^2.              (6)

They are +infinity outside that domain. These formulas follow by projecting
the initial y-coordinate -7 onto y>=-r for A and onto
y>=max(-r,1-t-4r/3) for B. At r=0 both reduce to (1), while at the
actual raised minimum r=19/24 and t=5/24 they give the two different
old-coordinate costs in (3).

## 3. Exact finite update with global recentering allowed

Take any old J_old=max(0,L_1,...,L_M) with min J_old=0. Let its entire
old ambient space contain x_init, p, u, every old normal and every old
proximal point z_i. The retained samples have heights V_i=J_old(z_i),
and the boundary query is p-m_boundary u, m_boundary>0. Retain Phi,
Psi as in (1) and Xi as in (5). No assumption about a small state size
is made.

Specify finite new-cell normals (a,-q), a>0, 0<=q<=1, including a single
q=0 cap (c,0) and endpoint (epsilon,-1). The local queries (u_j,-y_j)
and selected normals (a_j,-q_j) obey their prescribed GD differences and
all local support inequalities, with terminal query and selected normal
(epsilon,-1). Write

    U_j=u_j-a_j,
    h_j=< (a_j,-q_j),(U_j,-(y_j-q_j)) > >=0,
    r_0=(R_x,-R_y),   lambda=sqrt(1+epsilon^2).

A supplied bridge b>1 and scale d>0 determine

    theta=(b-1)m_boundary-d R_x.

As in the current joining geometry require theta>=0. Choose F_cell>0,
and a new unit coordinate e orthogonal to the entire old ambient. Put

    p_new=p+theta u+d R_y e,
    L_(a,q)=F_cell+d<a u-qe,z-p_new>,
    Jbar=max(J_old,all L_(a,q)),
    u_new=(-epsilon u+e)/lambda,
    m_new=d lambda.

The new query/proximal data are

    x_j=p_new+d(u_j u-y_j e),
    g_j=d(a_j u-q_j e),
    z_j=p_new+d(U_j u-(y_j-q_j)e),
    V_j=F_cell+d^2 h_j.

The complete two-direction interpolation test is exactly

    max_j[Phi(theta+d U_j)-d^2 h_j] <= F_cell
       <= min_(a,q)[Psi(d a)+d a theta-d^2 R_y q].         (7)

An old plane at a new z_j depends only on its old projection
p+(theta+d U_j)u, giving the left side. A new plane at an old z_i is
F_cell+d a(<u,z_i-p>-theta)+d^2 R_y q, giving the right side.
Together with the supplied local inequalities this checks every pair.
It gives the proximal data for the same single Jbar, without requiring
that Jbar still have a zero.

The unrecentered outgoing and acceptance profiles are

    Phibar(tau)=max{Phi(theta-epsilon tau/lambda),
                     F_cell+max_(a,q)[-d(epsilon a+q)tau/lambda]},

    Psibar(s)=min{Psi(-epsilon s/lambda)
                            +s(d R_y-epsilon theta)/lambda,
                 min_j[F_cell+d^2h_j
                            +s d(epsilon U_j+y_j-q_j)/lambda]}. (8)

For each real r set

    Z_r(t)=max_(a,q),q>0[d R_y+(F_cell-r)/(d q)
                                      +(a/q)(t-theta)],
    w(t,tau)=lambda tau+d R_y+epsilon(t-theta).

The exact sublevel-distance update is

    Xibar(tau,r)=inf_t {Xi(t,r)+w(t,tau)^2:
        t<=theta+(r-F_cell)/(d c), w(t,tau)>=Z_r(t)}.       (9)

This follows by writing an enlarged point as z=z_old+w e. Its old
coordinate t=<u,z_old-p> must obey J_old(z_old)<=r. The cap gives the
upper bound on t, each positive-q plane gives one lower bound on w,
and fixing the new outgoing slice determines w=w(t,tau). Orthogonality
to x_init as well as the entire old ambient gives the squared-distance
sum. Conversely an attaining old point for Xi(t,r), with that appended
w, realizes exactly the displayed cost. Thus (9) is an equality, including
empty cases; finite minima on fixed new slices are attained by closedness
and coercivity.

Since Jbar is the maximum of finitely many affine functions, includes zero,
and is finite, its minimum mu>=0 is attained. One elementary way to see
attainment is to project its nonempty epigraph polyhedron onto the value
coordinate; Fourier--Motzkin elimination gives a polyhedron in R, and
the projection is closed and bounded below. Equivalently, using (9),

    mu=min{r>=0: Xibar(tau,r)<infinity for some tau}.       (10)

Now recenter the WHOLE function by J_new=Jbar-mu. Its exact new state is

    Phi_new=Phibar-mu,  Psi_new=Psibar-mu,
    Xi_new(tau,r)=Xibar(tau,r+mu),  r>=0.                 (11)

All old and new proximal heights are reduced by the same mu; gradients
and iterates do not change. As Jbar>=mu everywhere, inserting the zero
plane into the maximum of all shifted planes leaves J_new unchanged.
The boundary gradient magnitude remains m_new. In particular the exact
normalized endpoint error is

    [2(F_cell-mu)+d^2(1+epsilon^2)] / min_tau Xibar(tau,mu). (12)

The denominator is the distance to an actual closest minimizer of the
same function whose gradients realize the entire supplied history.

This is a finite rule. Xi is a convex extended-real piecewise quadratic
function of (t,r): fix any active face of the linearly parameterized
polyhedron defining (5); its equality-constrained Euclidean projection
is affine in (t,r), and its squared distance is quadratic. Primal and
normal-cone conditions select polyhedral parameter regions. There are
finitely many active subsets; if a subset is dependent, retain a basis
for the affine hull and describe its normal cone with the full active
set. This does not require nondegeneracy. On every piece, (9) minimizes
a quadratic in one scalar t over linear inequalities in (t,tau,r).
The positive coefficient from the fixed t-slice squared distance permits
the unconstrained affine vertex to be clipped to the feasible interval.
Checking the finitely many pieces gives another finite piecewise quadratic
profile. No solver or numerical sweep is part of the construction.

## 4. In the arc-chain regime the amount of recentering is scalar

There is a useful exact consequence when the old zero-slice domain is
[F_old/m_boundary,infinity), where F_old=J_old(p)>0. Assume also that
-m_boundary u is an active old boundary normal. For every
0<=r<=F_old,

    {t:Xi(t,r)<infinity}=[(F_old-r)/m_boundary,infinity).   (13)

The supporting plane gives the lower bound. If r<F_old and t is at
least that bound, take a zero point with outgoing coordinate
t_zero=t F_old/(F_old-r), and form the convex combination with p whose
weight on that zero point is (F_old-r)/F_old. Its coordinate is t and
its value is at most r. If r=F_old, use p when t=0, and for t>0 mix p
with any zero point at a coordinate at least max(t,F_old/m_boundary).
This proves every claimed feasible slice without using a distance bound.

Assume the cross-tests (7) hold. Let R_cap=d c. Then the actual minimum
in (10) is the explicit value

    mu=max(0,[R_cap F_old+m_boundary F_cell
                  -m_boundary R_cap theta]/[m_boundary+R_cap]). (14)

To prove it, for any r<=min(F_old,F_cell) the old sublevel is feasible
at exactly the t in (13). The new cap requires
t<=theta-(F_cell-r)/R_cap. Every positive-q plane can be satisfied
by making w sufficiently large. Thus feasibility is equivalent to

    (F_old-r)/m_boundary+(F_cell-r)/R_cap <= theta.

The displayed root is no greater than F_old because the new cap at p
is at most F_old. It is no greater than F_cell because the old boundary
plane at p_new is at most F_cell. These are included in (7), so the
calculation applies at the claimed nonnegative minimum itself. This
proves both the lower bound and attainment in (14).

For a concave-arc cell satisfying

    a-epsilon q>=0,
    (a-epsilon q)/c+q>=1,

the endpoint lower bound on w dominates every other positive-q bound
on the cap-feasible range whenever r<=F_cell. Subtract the endpoint
bound from a general bound and use
t-theta<=-(F_cell-r)/(d c); the result is at most
(F_cell-r)/(d q)[1-q-(a-epsilon q)/c]<=0.
Consequently the new zero-slice domain after (11) is exactly
[(F_cell-mu)/(d lambda),infinity). The domain hypothesis used in
(13) is therefore preserved by these joins, even when mu>0.

In particular a positive minimum does not make the geometric join
illegal. It consumes function-value height, with the exact identity

    (F_old-mu)/m_boundary+(F_cell-mu)/R_cap=theta          (15)

whenever the positive part in (14) is active. The earlier zero-preserving
budget was the condition mu=0. Allowing mu>0 requires the sublevel
distance state, as the counterexample proves; it does not erase the
loss or determine its normalization from Dist alone.

## 5. Remaining quantitative question

This package gives an actual larger class of legal iterative joins and
an exact, growing finite state. Cross-history legality (7), the loss (14),
and the nearest-minimizer cost (9) all remain in the same construction.
A policy selecting cells, scales and levels for every prescribed schedule
with normalized endpoint error at least (1-o(1))U_n^ZJ is still absent.
None of the displayed example ratios is claimed to optimize W_n.
All new assertions here are research findings awaiting verification;
they are not accepted graph facts or premises for other submissions.

claim: C15 robust scalar obstruction: actual ray derivatives may be asymmetric and nonperiodic, with arbitrary horizon-dependent knots, provided both lie between (97/100)G_ref and G_ref for one monotone 1-Lipschitz reference satisfying G_ref((13/5)R)=(13/5)G_ref(R). On H_m every such actual trajectory has normalized gap <=(1/(a c))c^(-m), uniformly o(U_(2^m-1)^ZJ). evidence:
# A robust scalar clock obstruction with asymmetric nonperiodic derivatives

Status: complete candidate proof, unverified. No fact_submit is allocated to
this lane. Every ingredient used below is proved here; earlier unverified
findings are motivation only. This is a bound on a specified scalar function
class, not on all scalar functions and not on unrestricted multidimensional W.

## 1. The class and the bound

Set c=13/5, a=c^(-17), b_j=a c^j, and

    H_0=(),   H_(j+1)=(H_j,b_j,H_j),
    N_j=2^j-1,   s_j=sum H_j=a(c^j-2^j)/(c-2).

Let G_ref:[0,infinity)->[0,infinity) be nondecreasing and 1-Lipschitz,
G_ref(0)=0, and G_ref(cR)=c G_ref(R) for every R>=0. This is a reference profile,
not necessarily the derivative used by GD. Put kappa=97/100.

Independently choose two nondecreasing 1-Lipschitz functions g_+,g_- on
[0,infinity), both zero at zero, satisfying

    kappa G_ref(R) <= g_sigma(R) <= G_ref(R),   R>=0, sigma in {+,-}.  (1)

Define the single fixed function used by the algorithm by

    f(x)=integral_0^x g_+(t)dt                     if x>=0,
    f(x)=integral_0^(-x) g_-(t)dt                 if x<=0.     (2)

Its derivative is g_+(x) on the positive ray and -g_-(-x) on the negative
ray. It is continuous, nondecreasing and globally 1-Lipschitz: across zero,
g_+(R)+g_-(T)<=R+T. Thus f is finite, convex, differentiable and 1-smooth,
with f(0)=0=min f. It need not be even and neither g_sigma need satisfy
any radial scaling identity.

For every m>=17 and every x_0!=0, run GD on this same f with the full
predetermined schedule H_m. Then

    2 f(x_(N_m))/|x_0|^2 <= (1/(a c)) c^(-m).               (3)

All choices in (1), including the reference G_ref, may depend on m. In
particular, the number of knots, their locations, ray asymmetry and
nonperiodic changes can depend on the horizon. The constant in (3) is
independent of these choices.

The ratio of the supremum in (3) to the exact U_(N_m)^ZJ tends to zero.
An elementary estimate for that exact profile is proved in Section 5.

## 2. Quantitative closure for the reference clock

If G_ref is identically zero, (1) makes the objective zero. Otherwise G_ref(R)>0
for all R>0. Indeed, a zero at one positive radius, monotonicity and discrete
homogeneity would force zeros on arbitrarily large intervals. Define

    M_ref=max_(R>0) G_ref(R)/R,    ell_ref=1/M_ref,
    Clock_ref(R)=integral_1^R dt/G_ref(t),   R>0.

The ratio G_ref(R)/R is continuous and periodic under R->cR, so its positive
maximum exists on a compact radial period. Smoothness gives ell_ref>=1.
The clock Clock_ref is strictly increasing. Substitution t=cu gives a constant

    tau_ref=Clock_ref(cR)-Clock_ref(R)>0,                                    (4)

independent of R. Choose r>=17 minimal with b=b_r>=ell_ref. Thus

    b/c<ell_ref<=b.

Define

    D_ref=max_(R>0) [Clock_ref(b G_ref(R))-Clock_ref(R)].     (5)

The expression is continuous and radially periodic, so its maximum exists.
At a point attaining M_ref, b G_ref(R)>=R. Hence D_ref>=0.

We first prove

    tau_ref+D_ref <= (c-1)b.                                     (6)

Fix R>0, put u=G_ref(R)>0 and q=R/u>=1. If q<=b, monotonicity gives
Clock_ref(bu)-Clock_ref(R)<=(b-q). On [R,cR], the endpoint values u,cu and the
1-Lipschitz condition give

    G_ref(t)>=max(u, cu-(cR-t)).

The switch is at cR-(c-1)u, inside [R,cR]. Integration of the reciprocal
therefore yields

    tau_ref <= (c-1)(q-1)+log c.

Adding proves

    tau_ref+Clock_ref(bu)-Clock_ref(R)
      <= b+(c-2)q-(c-1)+log c < (c-1)b,

because q<=b, c>2 and log c<c-1. If q>=b, instead write the expression as
Clock_ref(cbu)-Clock_ref(R). When cbu<R it is negative. Otherwise G_ref(t)>=u on its integration
interval, so it is at most cb-q<=(c-1)b. This proves (6) after maximizing.

We need the slightly stronger block budget

    kappa s_r >= tau_ref+D_ref.                                 (7)

For r>=18, use (10/13)^18<1/100. One direct exact check is
13^9=10604499373>10^10, followed by squaring. Consequently

    s_r/b_r = [1-(10/13)^r]/(3/5) > 33/20,
    kappa s_r/b_r > (97/100)(33/20)=3201/2000>8/5=c-1.

This and (6) imply (7). If r=17, then b=1 and ell_ref=1. In that case G_ref is
identically R: a radius R_0 attaining G_ref(R_0)=R_0 forces G_ref(t)=t on
[0,R_0] by the Lipschitz bound in both directions; discrete homogeneity
extends this to every radius. Thus tau_ref=log c and D_ref=0. Also s_17>=13/8:
indeed (10/13)^3<1/2 and (10/13)^2<4/5 give (10/13)^17<1/40.
It follows that kappa s_17>=1261/800>1>log(13/5), proving (7) here too.
For the last strict inequality, exp(1)>1+1+1/2+1/6=8/3>13/5.

## 3. Updates for the actual, possibly nonperiodic and asymmetric function

Every step h within H_r is at most b/c<ell_ref. By (1), g_sigma(R)<=R/ell_ref,
so such a step preserves the sign and sends R to

    R'=R-hg_sigma(R)>0.

Monotonicity of the reference G_ref and the lower inequality in (1) give

    Clock_ref(R)-Clock_ref(R')
       >= (R-R')/G_ref(R)
       = h g_sigma(R)/G_ref(R) >= kappa h.                    (8)

Therefore every full copy of H_r decreases this same clock by at least
kappa s_r, regardless of which ray it visits or how many gradient knots
it traverses. This is an estimate on the actual fixed-function trajectory.

A checkpoint of level k has step h=b c^k. If it changes sign, its next
radius satisfies

    R'=b c^k g_sigma(R)-R <= c^k b G_ref(R).

Using (4)-(5),

    Clock_ref(R')-Clock_ref(R)<=k tau_ref+D_ref.                                 (9)

If it preserves the sign its radius decreases, so (9) still holds because
D_ref>=0. If a step lands at zero, all subsequent iterates are zero and (3)
holds immediately. No clock is evaluated at zero.

The same reference clock is used on both rays. There is no assumption
equating the two actual derivatives, their areas, or their scale periods.

## 4. Sum the exact word and retain the complete objective

Suppose m>=r and put J=m-r and S=s_r. The word H_m contains 2^J copies of
H_r and 2^J-1 checkpoints. Level k occurs 2^(J-k-1) times for 0<=k<J.
Their sum of levels is 2^J-J-1 (obtained, for example, by induction on J).
Summing (8)-(9) along the original trajectory gives the explicit recurrence
bound

    Clock_ref(|x_(N_m)|)-Clock_ref(|x_0|)
      <= -2^J kappa S+(2^J-J-1)tau_ref+(2^J-1)D_ref
      = -2^J(kappa S-tau_ref-D_ref)-(J+1)tau_ref-D_ref
      <= -(J+1)tau_ref.                                     (10)

By (4) and strict monotonicity of Clock_ref,

    |x_(N_m)|<=c^(-J-1)|x_0|.                            (11)

Every function-value area in (2) is included; (1) gives the global bound

    f(x)<=integral_0^|x| G_ref(t)dt <= |x|^2/(2ell).

As ell_ref>b/c,

    2f(x_(N_m))/|x_0|^2
       <= ell_ref^(-1)c^(-2J-2)
       <= b^(-1)c^(-2J-1)
       = a^(-1)c^(-m-J-1) <= (1/(a c))c^(-m).

If 17<=m<r, every step is less than ell_ref. The entire trajectory stays on
its initial ray with decreasing radius. Write R=|x_(N_m)| and
w=g_sigma(R). Monotonicity gives

    R+s_m w<=|x_0|.

Smoothness and monotonicity also give g_sigma(t)<=min(t,w) for 0<=t<=R,
so f(x_(N_m))<=Rw-w^2/2. Completing the square proves

    2f(x_(N_m))/|x_0|^2 <= 1/(1+2s_m)
       <= (1/(2(13/8)a))c^(-m) <= (1/(a c))c^(-m).

Here s_m>=(13/8)a c^m follows from the calculation for m>=17 above.
This completes (3) for every allowed m. Multiplication of f by any L>0
gives the same normalized ratio and the identical GD trajectory with steps
h_t/L, so the result uses exactly the project's normalization.

## 5. Comparison to the exact Zhang--Jiang profile

Use the exact sequences in PROBLEM.md, with C_n=S_circle(n)+1 and
B_n=2S_bullet(n)+1, so U_n^ZJ=1/B_n. Their shifted join maps are

    Omega(A,B)=(A+B+sqrt((A+B)^2+4AB))/2,
    Gamma(A,B)=2A+B/2+sqrt(B^2+8AB)/2.

For nonnegative A,B,

    Omega(A,B)<=(A^(3/4)+B^(3/4))^(4/3).                   (12)

To check (12), normalize A^(3/4)+B^(3/4)=1, write
A=t^(4/3), B=(1-t)^(4/3), and compare 1 with the positive root of
z^2-(A+B)z-AB. The needed inequality is
t^(4/3)+(1-t)^(4/3)+[t(1-t)]^(4/3)<=1. Put
x=t^(1/3), y=(1-t)^(1/3). Its difference from 1 is

    x^3 y^3 [1/(1+x+x^2)+1/(1+y+y^2)-xy]>=0,

since each reciprocal is at least 1/3 and xy<=2^(-2/3)<2/3.
The case A=B=0 holds directly. Induction in the primitive DP gives
C_n<=(n+1)^(4/3). Next Gamma(A,B)<=B+4A, by squaring
sqrt(B^2+8AB)<=B+4A. Induction in the dominant DP, and
u^(4/3)+v^(4/3)<=(u+v)^(4/3), give

    B_n<=1+4n^(4/3).                                     (13)

The superadditive power inequality follows, for example, by differentiating
(u+v)^p-u^p in v for p=4/3 and comparing its derivative to p v^(p-1).
Thus the ratio in question is at most

    (1/(a c)) c^(-m) [1+4(2^m-1)^(4/3)] -> 0,

because c^3=2197/125>16. This is an exact-profile comparison, not an appeal
to a decimal asymptotic coefficient or a computation over finitely many m.

## 6. Explicit deformations and finite trajectory-preserving versions

The class has genuinely nonperiodic members. Choose measurable functions
w_sigma(t) in [kappa,1], independently on the two rays, and set

    g_sigma(R)=integral_0^R w_sigma(t) G_ref'(t)dt,
    f(sigma R)=integral_0^R (R-t) w_sigma(t) G_ref'(t)dt.        (14)

The derivative G_ref' exists almost everywhere, lies in [0,1], and integrates
to G_ref because G_ref is Lipschitz. Formula (14) gives (1) and proves the required
monotonicity and Lipschitz bounds directly. A piecewise constant w_sigma
with arbitrary breakpoints yields independent spatial changes; no periodic
pattern of those breakpoints is required. The choices are made once for the
entire run and the integral in (14) is the complete function value.

If G_ref is piecewise affine with finitely many pieces in one radial period,
and each w_sigma has finitely many pieces on every compact subinterval of
(0,infinity), any finite trajectory avoiding zero has an equivalent legal
finite-knot realization. On each ray choose R below every nonzero sampled
radius on that ray, and set u=g_sigma(R), A=f(sigma R). Then

    u^2/2<=A<=Ru-u^2/2.

The lower bound follows from g_sigma(t)>=max(0,u-(R-t)); the upper bound
from g_sigma(t)<=min(t,u). Set delta=R-u/2-A/u. The bounds say
0<=delta<=R-u. Replace the inner ray by zero up to delta, a unit-slope ramp
of length u, then a plateau of height u up to R. Its endpoint gradient
remains u and its area is Ru-delta u-u^2/2=A. All larger gradients and
values are unchanged. If a ray is never queried, choose any such R or
retain a simple legal zero derivative there. Cap the outer derivative after
all sampled radii. The two ray replacements join legally at the same
minimizer zero and preserve the actual GD trajectory, all sampled values,
and the original initial distance. The number of retained pieces may grow
with m. An arbitrary unrelated replacement is not asserted to obey (3).

## 7. Boundary of this result

This removes evenness and exact radial homogeneity from the actual
objective, and it allows unbounded geometric complexity. It retains a
specific global restriction: both ray derivatives must lie in the common
relative band (1) beneath one discretely homogeneous reference profile.
It is not a bound on every asymmetric function or on every nonperiodic
profile. A future scalar witness at the benchmark scale must evade this
uniform band condition (or its trajectory-preserving finite versions).
The general scalar question and the all-schedule, all-dimensional exact
minimax target remain open.

claim: C16 removes the exact-gradient-grid assumption from the multiscale relay obstruction. For every fixed scalar smooth convex function on H_m, if every coarse checkpoint crosses, no H_r crosses internally, and initial-ray H_r blocks are flat, arbitrary nonperiodic plateau heights and arbitrary opposite-ray gradient variation still give normalized gap <=[(b-1)^2/((S+1)^2(2S+1))](1+S/b)^(2-2J)=O(c^(-m))=o(U_(2^m-1)^ZJ). evidence:
# Arbitrary nonperiodic flat-block relays lose a canonical plateau rank

Status: complete candidate proof, not verifier-accepted. No new verification
call is allocated. The proof is self-contained and does not use earlier
unverified conclusions as premises. It removes the geometric gradient-grid
hypothesis from the previous relay obstruction, replacing it by flatness of
the positive ordinary blocks. Negative ordinary blocks may vary arbitrarily.
It does not cover all scalar functions or unrestricted multidimensional W.

## 1. Statement and the exact class

Set c=13/5, a=c^(-17), b_j=a c^j, and

    H_0=(),   H_(j+1)=(H_j,b_j,H_j),
    N_j=2^j-1,   s_j=sum H_j=a(c^j-2^j)/(c-2).

Fix integers m>r>=18. Put J=m-r, b=b_r, S=s_r, eta=13/8, and

    gamma_rank=1+S/b.

The schedule H_m is exactly 2^J copies of H_r separated by checkpoints.
Their levels form the word

    T_0=(),   T_(j+1)=(T_j,j,T_j),

where level ell means step b c^ell. The zero-based even positions in this
checkpoint word all have level zero. Its odd positions have levels at least
one. There are 2^(J-1) positive ordinary blocks if the trajectory starts
positive and every checkpoint changes sign.

Consider any fixed differentiable convex scalar f with 1-Lipschitz
derivative, f(0)=0=min f, and a GD trajectory starting at x_0>0. Assume:

1. Every displayed checkpoint strictly changes sign, and no step inside a
   displayed H_r changes sign or reaches zero.
2. On every positive H_r block, the derivative is one positive constant
   throughout its traversed interval, including the checkpoint query at its
   end. The constant may differ between blocks and may be revisited later.

There is no restriction on the derivative variation within negative H_r
blocks, beyond legality of the same fixed function and condition 1. There
is no symmetry, homogeneity, geometric gradient grid, prescribed curvature
pattern, bound on the number of knots, or nested-return assumption.

For every such trajectory,

    2 f(x_(N_m))/x_0^2
      <= [(b-1)^2/((S+1)^2(2S+1))] gamma_rank^(2-2J)
      <= [c/(2 eta^3 a)] c^(-m).                         (1)

The bound is uniform in r, f, all plateau heights and locations, the number
of distinct plateaus and every revisit pattern. These may all depend on m.
The supremum of the left side over the specified class, divided by the exact
U_(N_m)^ZJ, tends to zero. Reflection gives the same statement with the two
rays interchanged, provided flatness is imposed on the initial ray.

## 2. The canonical intervals are intervals of one fixed derivative

If the terminal gap is zero, (1) holds directly. Otherwise no iterate is a
minimizer: a zero derivative would make all later iterates identical.
Write g_+(R)=f'(R) and g_-(R)=-f'(-R) for R>=0. Both are nonnegative,
nondecreasing, 1-Lipschitz and bounded above by R.

Index the positive ordinary blocks in time order by i=0,...,2^(J-1)-1.
Let u_i>0 be the constant derivative on block i, R_i its final radius
immediately before the low checkpoint b, and A_i its initial radius. Then

    A_i=R_i+S u_i,       R_i>=u_i,       R_i<b u_i.          (2)

The last inequality is exactly the strict sign change at that checkpoint.
The full interval [R_i,A_i] has derivative u_i by assumption.

Let U_flat be the finite set of distinct positive numbers occurring among
the u_i. For u in U_flat define

    L_flat(u)=min_{i:u_i=u} R_i,
    A_flat(u)=L_flat(u)+S u.                              (3)

These are canonical representatives for the whole finite trajectory, not
new points chosen independently at later times. The minimum is attained
at an actual visit. Therefore the interval

    [L_flat(u),A_flat(u)]

is a genuine flat interval of the fixed derivative with value u. Also

    u<=L_flat(u)<bu,     A_flat(u)<(b+S)u.                 (4)

If u<v are distinct elements of U_flat, monotonicity forces

    A_flat(u)<L_flat(v).                                 (5)

Indeed every point with derivative u lies strictly to the left of every
point with derivative v. In particular, this applies to the two endpoints
in (5). From (4)-(5),

    A_flat(u)<A_flat(v)-S v
                < A_flat(v) b/(b+S).

Thus consecutive canonical radii obey the strict multiplicative separation

    A_flat(v)>gamma_rank A_flat(u)       whenever u<v.    (6)

This is the source of the discrete rank. The gradient heights themselves
are arbitrary and need not lie in any geometric grid. Visits at different
positions on the same plateau are harmless because (3) takes the minimum
over all of them, once and for all, within the fixed legal function.

For r>=18 we have S/b>=eta. A direct proof is
(10/13)^3<1/2, (10/13)^2<4/5, hence (10/13)^17<1/40, and

    S/b=[1-(10/13)^r]/(c-2)>= (39/40)/(3/5)=13/8.

In particular,

    gamma_rank>=21/8>c,       eta^2=169/64>c.              (7)

## 3. Exact transfer across a pair of checkpoints

Consider two successive positive ordinary blocks, of derivative values
u and v. The intervening checkpoints have levels (0,ell) with ell>=1.
Let R be the actual departure radius of the first positive block. After
the low checkpoint the negative landing radius is

    B=b u-R <= b u-L_flat(u).                            (8)

Let w>0 and T>0 be the derivative magnitude and radius at the end of the
negative H_r block. All earlier negative-block gradients are at least w.
Smoothness gives T>=w. Thus

    B>=T+S w >= (S+1)w.                                 (9)

The checkpoint b c^ell lands on the positive ray at the initial radius
A_next of the next positive block. Equations (8)-(9) give

    A_next=b c^ell w-T
       <= (b c^ell-1)w
       <= [(b c^ell-1)/(S+1)] [b u-L_flat(u)].              (10)

The next block's actual departure is at least L_flat(v), so
A_flat(v)<=A_next. Since L_flat(u)>=u,

    b u-L_flat(u)
       <= [(b-1)/(S+1)] [L_flat(u)+S u]
       = [(b-1)/(S+1)] A_flat(u).                        (11)

For clarity, multiplying (11) by S+1 and moving the left side to the
right gives exactly (S+b)[L_flat(u)-u]>=0.
Consequently,

    A_flat(v)/A_flat(u)
       <= [(b-1)(b c^ell-1)]/(S+1)^2
       < c^ell/eta^2 < c^(ell-1).                        (12)

This transfer uses no negative-ray plateau assumption. It includes all
negative-block gradient variation through the lower bound (9).

## 4. A rank decrement that sums over the ruler word

Order U_flat increasingly, and let rank_flat(u) be its position in this
finite ordered set, starting with rank zero. By (6), a positive rank
increase of p multiplies A_flat by more than gamma_rank^p.

For a transition in (12),

    rank_flat(v)-rank_flat(u)<=ell-2.                     (13)

If ell=1, (12) gives A_flat(v)<A_flat(u), so v<u and the rank decreases
by at least one. If ell>=2, a rank increase of at least ell-1 would force
A_flat(v)/A_flat(u)>gamma_rank^(ell-1)>c^(ell-1), contradicting (12).
Zero or negative rank changes already satisfy (13) in this second case.

The positive-to-positive transitions use precisely the odd-indexed
checkpoints of T_J. A level ell>=1 occurs 2^(J-ell-1) times, for
1<=ell<=J-1. Their rank increments sum to at most

    sum_(ell=1)^(J-1) (ell-2)2^(J-ell-1)=1-J.             (14)

For J=1 the sum is empty and equals zero. To check (14) for all J, the
count is 2^(J-1)-1 and the sum of their levels is 2^J-J-1; subtract twice
the former from the latter. Both identities follow by doubling T_(J-1)
and inserting the new level J-1.

Let u_first and u_last be the derivatives of the first and last positive
ordinary blocks. Equations (6), (13)-(14) imply

    A_flat(u_last)<=gamma_rank^(1-J) A_flat(u_first)
                        <=gamma_rank^(1-J) x_0.          (15)

For J=1, the same positive block is both first and last, and the factor
is one. For J>1, the final rank is at least J-1 below the initial rank,
so the product of the intervening strict separations (6) proves (15).
The last inequality uses A_flat(u_first)<=A_0=x_0, a direct consequence
of the minimum defining L_flat.

## 5. Complete terminal area and uniformity

The last checkpoint is again b. Its negative landing radius B_last obeys,
by (8) and (11),

    B_last <= [(b-1)/(S+1)] A_flat(u_last).                (16)

The remaining negative H_r has no crossing. Let w=g_-(R) be its terminal
gradient magnitude and R its terminal radius. All earlier gradients in
that block are at least w, so R+S w<=B_last. Integrating the fixed derivative
on [0,R], the bound g_-(t)<=min(t,w) yields

    f(x_(N_m))<=Rw-w^2/2,
    2f(x_(N_m))<=2 B_last w-(2S+1)w^2
                          <=B_last^2/(2S+1).             (17)

Every inner function-value area is present in this inequality. Combining
(15)-(17) gives the first assertion in (1).

Since S>=eta b, its leading coefficient is bounded by 1/(2 eta^3 b).
Also J>=1 and gamma_rank>c, so gamma_rank^(2-2J)<=c^(2-2J). As m=r+J,

    [1/(2 eta^3 b)] c^(2-2J)
       = [1/(2 eta^3 a)] c^(-m) c^(2-J)
       <= [c/(2 eta^3 a)] c^(-m),                        (18)

as claimed. This is uniform when r and all function parameters vary with m.
Scaling f by L>0 makes its derivative L-Lipschitz and leaves the trajectory
unchanged for GD steps h_t/L. The normalized quantity in the project is
exactly the left side of (1). The fixed minimizer is always zero.

## 6. Exact-profile comparison without asymptotic numerical constants

Use the exact Zhang--Jiang DP definitions of PROBLEM.md. For
C_n=S_circle(n)+1 and B_n=2S_bullet(n)+1, their shifted joins are

    Omega(A,B)=(A+B+sqrt((A+B)^2+4AB))/2,
    Gamma(A,B)=2A+B/2+sqrt(B^2+8AB)/2.

The inequality Omega(A,B)<=(A^(3/4)+B^(3/4))^(4/3) for nonnegative A,B
can be checked after normalizing A^(3/4)+B^(3/4)=1. Set
A=t^(4/3), B=(1-t)^(4/3). Comparing 1 to the positive root of
z^2-(A+B)z-AB reduces the claim to

    t^(4/3)+(1-t)^(4/3)+[t(1-t)]^(4/3)<=1.

With x=t^(1/3), y=(1-t)^(1/3), the difference from 1 is
x^3 y^3[1/(1+x+x^2)+1/(1+y+y^2)-xy]>=0, since the reciprocal terms are
each at least 1/3 and xy<=2^(-2/3)<2/3. The zero case is direct.
Induction therefore gives C_n<=(n+1)^(4/3). Next Gamma(A,B)<=B+4A,
by squaring sqrt(B^2+8AB)<=B+4A. Induction in the dominant recursion
gives B_n<=1+4n^(4/3), using the superadditivity of the power 4/3 on
nonnegative numbers. That superadditivity follows by comparing the
derivatives of (u+v)^p-u^p and v^p in v when p=4/3.

Since U_n^ZJ=1/B_n, (18) divided by U_(N_m)^ZJ is at most

    [c/(2 eta^3 a)] c^(-m) [1+4(2^m-1)^(4/3)] ->0,

because c^3=2197/125>16.

## 7. What the construction must change next

The proposed nonperiodic staircase repair cannot evade this proof by
choosing irregular heights, adding more plateau levels, revisiting old
plateaus, or allowing arbitrary negative-ray curvature. Legal flat
positive blocks themselves create the separated canonical radii, and the
smallest checkpoints force their rank to decrease through the recursive
word. The exact gradient update is (12) and the integer update is (13).

The scope restriction is substantive: every coarse checkpoint must cross,
there must be no crossing inside H_r, and the initial-ray H_r blocks must
be flat through their checkpoint query. A construction with significant
initial-ray gradient variation or a different crossing pattern is outside
the theorem. No claim about the full scalar class or about W_(N_m)(H_m)
is made.

# Exact terminal response after a single overrelaxed burst

Status: self-contained UNVERIFIED candidate. No new fact_submit is allocated.
Only accepted facts 1252b8823bb5a290 and b98bb807d514e80d are used as
predecessors. The one-step identities below are proved inside this candidate.

## 1. Exact statement

Use the original W_n from fact 1252b8823bb5a290: the supremum of
2(f(x_n)-f_star)/(L||x_0-x_star||^2) over all finite-dimensional convex
L-smooth functions with a minimizer, for the supplied nonnegative GD schedule.
Define, for b>=0,

    r_one(b)=max{1/(1+2b),(b-1)^2}.

For every a>=2 and b>=0,

    W_2(a,b)=(a-1)^2 r_one(b).                           (1)

Consequently

    inf_(b>=0) W_2(a,b)=(a-1)^2/4,                       (2)

and b=3/2 is the UNIQUE minimizing final step. The same statements hold
if any number of zero steps are inserted before a, between a and b, or
after b. In particular a prefix of any length k>=1 containing exactly
one nonzero step a>=2 has optimized final value (a-1)^2/4.

## 2. One-step upper certificates for every nonnegative step

Normalize L=1 and x_star=g_star=f_star=0. Write x for the initial point,
u for its gradient, x_1=x-bu, and v for the terminal gradient. Use the
signed Q residuals defined in fact1252b8823bb5a290. Every actual instance
has all Q<=0.

For 0<=b<=3/2, put q_one=1/(1+2b). Direct expansion gives the FULL identity

    q_one||x||^2-2f_1+Q_(0,star)+Q_(1,star)+Q_(1,0)
      =q_one||x-(b+1/2)(u+v)||^2
         +(3-2b)||u-v||^2/4.                            (3)

For completeness, the left side after value cancellation is

    q_one||x||^2-<x,u+v>+||u||^2+||v||^2
                       +(2b-1)<u,v>.

The right side has the same coefficients, using
q_one(b+1/2)=1/2. Its residual coefficient is nonnegative in the
stated range. Thus 2f_1<=q_one||x||^2.

For 3/2<=b<=2, put r=b-1 in [1/2,1]. Another FULL identity is

    r^2||x||^2-2f_1
      +2r Q_(0,star)+2(1-r)Q_(1,star)+2r Q_(1,0)
      =||v+u-(1-r)x||^2+(2r-1)||x-u||^2.             (4)

All three multipliers and both square coefficients are nonnegative.
To check (4), its left quadratic is

    r^2||x||^2-2r<x,u>-2(1-r)<x,v>
                       +2r||u||^2+2<u,v>+||v||^2.

The expansion of the right side is identical. Hence
2f_1<=(b-1)^2||x||^2.

For b>=2, adding interpolation between x and its minimizer gives
<x,u>>=||u||^2, while smoothness gives ||u||<=||x||. Therefore

    ||x-bu||^2
      <=||x||^2+b(b-2)||u||^2
      <=(b-1)^2||x||^2.

Smoothness at the minimizer then gives the same bound on 2f_1.
These arguments include b=0 and both interval endpoints.

The comparison of the two branches is exact:

    (b-1)^2(1+2b)-1=b^2(2b-3).

Thus (3)-(4) and the distance argument prove W_1(b)<=r_one(b) for all b>=0.

## 3. Matching scalar one-step instances

The scalar quadratic x^2/2 starting at 1 gives normalized error (b-1)^2.
The even Huber function with derivative clamp(x,[-q_one,q_one]), where
q_one=1/(1+2b), gives initial gradient q_one and terminal point
1-bq_one=(b+1)/(1+2b)>=q_one. Its normalized terminal value is

    2q_one(1-bq_one)-q_one^2=q_one.

Both functions are globally convex and 1-smooth and minimized at zero.
This proves W_1(b)=r_one(b), including b=0.

## 4. The burst factor, with both inequalities

For any actual function and initial point, the distance argument in Section2
with a>=2 gives

    ||x_1-x_star||^2<=(a-1)^2||x_0-x_star||^2.

Apply the just-proved one-step upper bound at x_1 for step b. If x_1 is
already a minimizer, its subsequent objective gap is zero; otherwise the
one-step bound is directly applicable in its original normalization.
Thus W_2(a,b)<=(a-1)^2 r_one(b).

For the reverse inequality, fact b98bb807d514e80d applied to the cut at a
has prefix sum zero and suffix sum b. It yields

    W_2(a,b)>=(a-1)^2/(1+2b).

Independently x^2/2 starting at 1 gives exactly
(a-1)^2(b-1)^2. Taking the larger of these two legal lower bounds proves
(1). There is no exchange of an infimum with this maximum: the equality
holds for EVERY fixed b before any minimization is performed.

The first branch of r_one is strictly decreasing up to b=3/2. After
3/2 the second branch is strictly increasing. Their common value there
is 1/4. This proves (2) and uniqueness.

Zero steps leave all actual iterates unchanged; their exact compression
and restoration in the original normalization is part of accepted
fact1252b8823bb5a290. Therefore all the zero-insertion statements follow.

## 5. A single deterministic two-dimensional saddle instance

There is also one actual function that resists EVERY final step b and
attains (2) at 3/2; this is not a choice of scalar instance after seeing b.
Put A=a-1>=1 and c=A/4. Let B_a(0)=0 and

    B_a'(z)=max(-c,min(1,z)),
    Q(z)=z^2/2.

These are convex differentiable 1-smooth scalar functions. At z_0=1,
both gradients are 1 and the initial step a sends each coordinate to -A.
For B_a the gradient there is -c; for Q it is -A. Define one fixed product

    F(z_1,z_2)=(8/9)B_a(z_1/sqrt(8/9))
                       +(1/9)Q(z_2/sqrt(1/9)),
    x_0=(sqrt(8/9),sqrt(1/9)).

Its gradient is 1-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm, and ||x_0||=1.
After the burst, the scalar final positions are -A+bc and A(b-1).
At b=3/2 the B_a coordinate is -5A/8<=-A/4, so the two normalized
channel values are both A^2/4. Their derivatives with respect to b
are respectively -A^2/8 and A^2. Thus the weighted derivative is zero.

The first channel is convex in b. Taking its tangent at 3/2 and using
the exact quadratic second channel gives, for EVERY b>=0,

    2F(x_2(b)) >= A^2/4+(A^2/9)(b-3/2)^2.            (5)

At 3/2 equality holds. This constructs an explicit final-stage saddle
in dimension two with a quadratic penalty for deviations from the
optimal final step. Arbitrary L is restored by replacing F with L F.

## 6. Quantitative state-compression obstruction, sharpened

For the equal-length, equal-sum prefixes

    h_even=(2,...,2),       length k>=1,
    h_burst=(2k,0,...,0),   length k,

each step of h_even is distance nonexpansive by the same distance
calculation at a=2. Appending 3/2 and using (3) gives

    inf_b W_(k+1)(h_even,b)<=1/4.

The exact result here gives

    inf_b W_(k+1)(h_burst,b)=(2k-1)^2/4.               (6)

Thus the two optimized values differ for every k>=2 and their ratio is
at least (2k-1)^2. This replaces the older S^(2/3)/12 lower estimate for
the burst prefix by its exact value. It is still a restriction on
sum-only closure, not a general lower bound as a function of the horizon.

claim: Exact last-step design SDP candidate: keep the COMPLETE prefix, add one vector w orthogonal to g_k and gamma<=2delta_j+2<x_k-y_j,w>-||w||² for EVERY anchor. Its attained value equals inf_b>=0 W(h_pre,b); an attained full PSD dual recovers b as its equality multiplier and proves every optimum b>1.
